Balor.json.text:
Balor is an Irish god. He is also called Balar, Bolar, and Balor of the Evil Eye. He reigned as king of the Fomorians, the monstrous race who held Ireland before the first invaders. His daughter was the fair Eithne. A prophecy warned that a son born to Eithne would kill his grandfather. Balor locked Eithne in a tower so she would never meet a man. He hoped that this would spare his own life.

Balor's greed undid that plan. He stole the magical cow Glas Ghaibhleann from a smith. In the second battle of Mag Tuired, the hero Lugh struck Balor with a slingshot or a spear made by the smith god Goibniu. Lugh cut off Balor's head. Even in death, Balor's remaining eye could split boulders.

Monaghan describes the eye as a third eye in the middle of Balor's forehead. It spat flames and destruction. Four men had to lift its heavy lid. Anyone who met its gaze fell down helpless. Balor's consort Cethlion also had poisonous powers that killed the god Dagda.

Balor is linked to Mizen Head in County Cork and to Land's End in Wales. Some scholars read him as a sun god.

Banba.json.text:
Banba is an Irish goddess. She is one of three earth goddesses, with Fódla and Ériu, who met the Milesians. The Milesians were the mythological invaders seen as the first Irish Celts. According to the Book of Invasions, Banba met them at Slieve Mis in County Kerry. Some sources place her on the plain from which the hill of Tara rises. Banba offered the Milesians happiness and wealth if the land bore her name. The Milesians instead gave precedence to Ériu, who made the same promise from the hill of Uisneach.

Three gods or heroes are named as the husbands of the three goddesses. Banba's husband was Mac Cuill, whose name means son of Hazel. Hazel nuts were said to feed the salmon of wisdom. The pig is an emblem of Banba, and her name resembles the Irish word for piglet, banb.

Banba told the Milesians she had been in Ireland before the biblical Noah. Some versions say the Milesians banished her by singing spells against her. Her name survives today as a poetic name for Ireland.

Bademagu.json.text:
Bademagu is an Arthurian hero, also called Maelwas. He was the father of Meleagant, the king or god of the Otherworld. Meleagant carried off Queen Guinevere and meant to force her to become his consort. He held her, and the knight Kay, in the city of Gorre.

Lancelot, the queen's beloved, set out to free them. The knight Gawain accompanied him. The road to Gorre crossed a turbulent river. Gawain took a safer underwater route. Lancelot raced across a sword-sharp upper bridge and was deeply wounded. In that state Lancelot fought Meleagant. Bademagu, a kindly king, forced his son to return the kidnapped queen.

Bairrind.json.text: Bairrind is an Irish mythological being. She was one of the women who traveled to Ireland with Cesair. Cesair fled the biblical Flood and arrived before the waters covered the earth. Three men sailed with the fifty women. In the Book of Invasions, Bith took Bairrind as his primary bride. So paired, Bith and Bairrind echoed the better-known trio of the goddesses Banba, Fódla, and Ériu.

Ban_Naemha.json.text: Ban Naemha is an Irish mythological being, also spelled Ban Naema. It is a magical fish of wisdom. It swims in a holy well. In Cork, the sun-well called Kil-na-Greina was its home. Only those gifted with second sight could see Ban Naemha. A ritual surrounded the well. People took three sips of the water. They crawled around the well three times between each drink. They offered a stone the size of a dove's egg with each circuit. Whether the ritual aimed to lure the fish or to honor the place is unclear.
